title: Fractal dimension predicts quantum kernel collapse in angle-encoded data
abstract: Angle-encoded quantum kernels on tabular data collapse when the feature map is wider than the intrinsic dimension of the data. We propose the correlation fractal dimension D2 as an a priori qubit budget: encode D2 coordinates chosen by FD-ASE instead of the PCA-95% width or all E attributes. On nine data sets and a statevector simulator (n= 32), a one-layer ZZ fidelity kernel at q=D2 stays geometrically alive while the same kernel at the PCA-95% width has already collapsed. The budget is map-dependent: product-state and IQP maps overshoot it; a second ZZ layer undershoots it. Packed dense-angle and re-uploading encodings still live at the fractal q, but not when PCA-95% features are stacked onto those qubits. Shrinking the angle bandwidth moves the ZZ knee later; stretching it kills the kernel earlier. On IBM Quantum (ibm_fez, 256 shots, n=8) the one-layer ZZ kernel at the fractal width matches the exact kernel (MAE 0.021); past that width both hardware and simulator have collapsed. The ceiling is a property of the map-data pair at a stated bandwidth, not of the classical table alone.
summary: This paper addresses kernel collapse in quantum machine learning by proposing that the correlation fractal dimension ($D_2$) dictates the maximum usable number of qubits. The authors demonstrate that using $D_2$ as a budget keeps the quantum kernel functional on both simulators and hardware, whereas over-encoding using methods like PCA causes the kernel to collapse.
main_problem: Quantum kernel methods applied to tabular data suffer from 'kernel collapse' when the feature map width exceeds the data's true intrinsic dimension.
main_result: The correlation fractal dimension ($D_2$) provides a superior, data-driven estimate for the optimal qubit budget, keeping the quantum kernel 'geometrically alive' where standard methods like PCA fail.
method: The authors use the correlation fractal dimension ($D_2$) derived from the data to set an a priori qubit budget, comparing the resulting quantum kernel fidelity against those derived from PCA or all attributes.
model_or_system: The model involves constructing quantum feature maps ($\vert\psi(x)angle$) using rotations on qubits (e.g., ZZ map) to define a quantum kernel $K_{ij} = \langle\psi(x_i) | \psi(x_j)angle$ for classification on tabular data.
key_observables: Kernel fidelity, the 'knee' width (last usable qubit count), and the ratio of nearest-neighbor to farthest-pair kernel similarities ($	ext{near}/	ext{far}$).
important_parameters: The correlation fractal dimension ($D_2$), the bandwidth ($c$), and the specific feature map used (e.g., ZZ layer depth).
main_assumptions: The optimal qubit budget is determined by the fractal dimension, and the kernel's usability is defined by maintaining specific structural inequalities (the 'alive' criterion).
figures_summary: Figures compare the measured kernel fidelity (MAE) and the mean off-diagonal elements of the kernel matrix across various feature map widths, showing a clear collapse past the fractal dimension limit.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of kernel collapse, proposes $D_2$ as the solution, validates this budget using multiple datasets and map types (ZZ, IQP), and confirms the findings using both quantum simulators and actual quantum hardware measurements.
why_interesting: The work provides a rigorous, information-theoretic measure ($D_2$) to guide the design of quantum circuits for data encoding, directly addressing the resource scaling problem in QML.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: A point on the dotted y = x line means the proposed ceiling equals the knee of the fidelity kernel (PCA view, one-layer ZZ, n = 32; knee = last alive q, Section 2.5). Left: ⌈D2⌉sits next to that knee (breast on the line at 3; pendigits 6 vs. 5). Centre: TwoNN [Facco et al., 2017] overshoots moons/intrinsic2 (≈13) because it treats embedding noise as extra dimension. Right: PCA-95% asks for 10–40 qubits while the kernel has already died at q ≤5—that panel has its own x-axis so the live knees (2–7) remain visible. Outliers we report as failures: onebig (kernel lives past the ceiling), wine/diabetes (high ID, n = 32 dies early), digits (unreliable box-count).

Figure 2: Breast cancer (E = 30, D2 ≈2.49). Dotted vertical: fractal budget q = 3. Grey dashed: PCA-95% (q = 10). Solid lines: fidelity kernel (the QML object). Dashed lines: classical RBF on the same coordinates (control). Mean off-diagonal (top centre): every fidelity curve falls toward 0 as q grows—states become orthogonal; RBF does not, so this is the feature map, not classical high dimension. near/far, kNN, SVM F1: on the PCA view of the fidelity kernel the usable geometry and the QML scores peak at the knee q = 3 and degrade past it. Figure 3: Mean off-diagonal of K versus q at four bandwidths. Dotted vertical: ⌈D2⌉. Dashed horizontal: the 0.03 alive floor. Open markers fail the alive rule. Smaller c (angles in [0, cπ]) delays collapse; c = 1 is the default ZZ scale.
Figure 4: Last alive q over ten kernel samples (n = 32, PCA, one-layer ZZ, c = 1). Median 3 on both breast and moons.

Figure 5: Packed encodings, simulator, n = 32. Y : mean off-diagonal of the fidelity kernel (higher = less collapsed). Teal: alive. Grey: dead. Dotted: 0.03 threshold. Left to right in each panel: ZZ at ⌈D2⌉; ZZ beyond it; dense-angle / re-upload of a few extra PCs on the fractal q; re-upload of a PCA-95%-scale feature count on that q. The last of those is grey: stacking extra coordinates onto fewer qubits is not a workaround.
